newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels can claim victories in 50-day-old siege.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels can claim victories in 50-day-old siege.

text.p: After 50 days in captivity, the 72 hostages held by Marxist rebels in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima appear little closer to freedom, but their captors have scored several public relations victories.

President Alberto Fujimori, buoyed by support from U.S. and Japanese leaders during visits to Canada and the United States, returned to Lima on Tuesday saying he would continue to show firmness and prudence in his bid to free the captives.

Prudence, analysts said, was likely to keep Fujimori from storming the residence for now. Firmness would keep him from caving in to the key demand of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) to free 400 jailed guerrillas.

"One thing is for sure, this is not going to be over soon unless the government takes a more robust approach, which appears unlikely to happen," David Lattin of Control Risks Group said in an interview from Washington. "And the MRTA doesn't get alarmed by time. They certainly have many precedents with kidnappings that demonstrate that."

The roughly 15 MRTA rebels who stormed the diplomatic compound on Dec. 17 were looking to obtain more than just the freedom of their fellow guerrillas. They have already claimed victory in the siege's first stage, which they have dubbed "Breaking the Silence" for the boost to the public profile of the group that all but disappeared in recent years.

And they have managed to draw the world's attention to the deplorable state of Peru's prisons, where the majority of their dwindling numbers linger, and to the administration's difficulty in wrestling unemployment and poverty lower.

"The rebels always ask for big things they never get. But they do obtain smaller things," Jorge Aragon of the consulting and polling firm Apoyo said. "They did return to the public debate and people are talking about prison reform."

Analysts suggested the rebels chose to attack the Japanese compound in part because they knew Tokyo, with a history of negotiating similar situations in the past, would push Fujimori to take a cautious approach. That would give the MRTA time to draw attention to their cause.
"They raised their public profile internationally, that's an achievement," Lattin said. "Two days before this few people knew about them abroad. Since then, their influence has been registered.
"If they are looking for the release of their guerrillas, it may not happen, but it's a starting point. Even if they manage to improve jail conditions, then that's a success."

The MRTA rebels seized hundreds of guests when they stormed the residence during a diplomatic reception. They released most but kept those they considered the most important bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother, top government officials, two ambassadors, and two dozen Japanese.

When Fujimori won 1990 elections against renowned novelist Mario Vargas Llosa, he gave virtual carte blanche to the military to crush the MRTA and what was then Peru's best-known guerrilla group, the Maoist Shining Path. The leaders of both groups were captured in 1992.

But Fujimori has been under pressure from Tokyo to reach a peaceful solution. Better known for strong-arm tactics than diplomacy, the son of Japanese immigrants has adopted a strategy of uncharacteristic restraint.
"This must be terrible for him," sociologist Guillermo Rochabru of Catholic University of Peru said. "He likes to be in complete control and is not accustomed to negotiating."
But surveys show public opinion is clearly in favour of a negotiated settlement.

"Fujimori has taken decisions that have been unpopular in the short term knowing they would turn around for him later on," pollster Aragon said. "But an unpopular decision on this (an attack) would not turn in his favour."
